utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mr. Waespi, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, legal assistant -- Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At today's hearing of the 1st of December, the Chamber bids good morning to all those present. The representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence, who are all present; the accused, and all the personnel in this courtroom. I understand Mr. Bourgon wants to take the floor and I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam Judge. Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President. Could we go into private session, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In open session, let me say that we are waiting for the arrival of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to check that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying into your own language. If so, say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I'd be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ermin Husejnagic. I was born on the 1st of January, 1960, in Zenica, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are you currently employed? Do you hold a position of any kind? And if so, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm employed in the Ministry of the Interior in the Zenica/Doboj Canton. I work as the chief in the forensics department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You work for the Ministry of the Interior in the Zenica/Doboj Canton? In what capacity, because I didn't receive the interpretation of that. What is your actual position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am the chief of the forensics department, which is part of the crime police of the Ministry of the Interior in the Zenica and Doboj Canton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1992 and 1993, that's over ten years ago, did you hold a position? And if so, what sort of position and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the time I also worked for the police. But it was in the CSB of Zenica, the security services centre in Zenica. I was involved in analysing mechanical traces at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before in an international or national court about the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I will be testifying about the events that took place in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a forensics expert, have you ever testified before the courts in your country about crimes and offences of various sorts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified about war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But have you ever testified about ordinary crimes, common law crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have testified on a number of occasions with regard to such crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Defence counsel for the examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information. You've told me that you have already testified before local courts as an expert, so you have met with the sort of questions that an expert witness might be asked. The procedure we follow here is different from the procedure followed in your country, but you will here have to answer questions that will first be put to you by Defence counsel, whom you have certainly met; they are to your left. The examination-in-chief should take between an hour and an hour and a half. I hope it will be less than an hour and a half. After that stage the Prosecution, who are to your right, will conduct their cross-examination. The questions they put to you will be put to you to verify your testimony and to clarify some of the answers that you've provided to Defence counsel. Once this stage has been completed, Defence counsel may re-examine you. Then the three Judges, who are sitting before you, and this must be the case in your country, too, may ask you other questions. As a rule, the Judges ask questions either to clarify your answers or they base their questions on the documents shown to you by the parties or they ask a witness questions because they feel there are certain gaps that need to be filled. Once the Judges have asked you questions and you have answered these questions, the parties may ask you additional questions. So this is how we will be proceeding, but you are certainly not very surprised by what I have told you, since you must be familiar with such procedure. I also want to point out two other things. As you have taken the solemn declaration, you should not give false testimony. A witness could be prosecuted for having given false testimony. I would also like to remind you that if when answering a question you believe that your answer could be used against you at a subsequent date, could be used to prosecute you at a subsequent date, you may refuse to answer the question. You have this right. A witness has the right not to answer certain questions, but in such an exceptional case it is possible for the Trial Chamber to oblige you to answer the question, but you are granted a form of immunity. This is a very particular situation, but I wanted to inform you of it. Certain technical matters will also be discussed. If you feel the question is too complicated, ask the party putting the question to you to rephrase it. We don't have any written documents, so your oral testimony is what is important. If you don't understand a question, ask the party putting it to you to rephrase the question. If you feel that there are any difficulties, inform us of the fact. Having provided you with this information, I will now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Husejnagic.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the information the Presiding Judge has just provided you with, I would like to add something else. We both speak the same language and you might want to answer my questions as soon as I put them to you, but it's necessary for my questions and your answers to be interpreted to enable everyone in the courtroom to follow us. This is why I would be grateful if you could make a brief pause after I have put my question to you, and only then should you answer the question. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, where do you live right now?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge you told us about your job, but tell me what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given your position, I will ask the registrar to make an order to delete the name of the street that you live in. Mr. Registrar, could you prepare an order to delete the witness's address that appears in lines 23 and 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a mechanical engineer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me something about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: After I had finished primary school I graduated from the mechanical engineering university in 1997. In 1997 I enrolled in the university for mechanical engineering and I graduated in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, as a mechanical engineer, what sort of work did you do before the war?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Before the war, I worked in the Zenica steelworks. I worked on mechanical design -- in the mechanical design field. This was in the work organisation -- in a work organisation in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, at any point in time did you start working for a different company and where did you find employment if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991 and at the very beginning of 1992 I left the Zenica steelworks and went to the Zenica CSB, security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, before you started performing these duties or at any other point in time did you serve in an army before the war, and if so, did you have a rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: After I have graduated, I went to the army, I went to the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and I didn't have a rank of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When at the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992 you moved to the CSB in Zenica, what duties did you perform there, or rather, did you obtain any other professional knowledge that related to your duties?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, on the very first day in the CSB, in Zenica, I went to Sarajevo, to the school in Vrace, to specialise there. This training was -- involved training in the field of forensics.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, where were you when the war broke out in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I was in Vraca in the school up until the 4th of April. On the 4th of April the blockade of Sarajevo started and it was no longer possible to reach Sarajevo. And it was particularly difficult to reach Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were an expert in the CSB. Who was your superior and which body was your superior body?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The chief of the forensics department was my superior, and the body concerned was the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1992 and in 1993, whose authority was the CSB under?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It was under the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, at any point in time in 1992 or 1993 did the BH army -- was the BH army a body that had authority over the CSB, or rather over the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: No. The BH army never had authority over the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, could you now tell me something about the organisation of the CSB. Or rather, how was work within the CSB divided?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The CSB had a crime police department, it had a uniformed police department, and it had an administration department, which had no authority. So their employees didn't have police authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, could you tell us who the members of the uniformed police were.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the members of the uniform police were police inspectors in the headquarters and then the support unit, a special unit, and all the policemen in the police stations covered by the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell me how the crime police department was organised.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The crime police department was organised on the basis of departments. Within the crime police department there was the department for offences, for commercial crime, and there was the forensics department.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a CSB employee, which department were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the forensics department.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said that you were an expert in mechanical traces. Tell me, what does the term -- what do the terms "mechanical traces" mean? What sort of work does this involve?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, mechanical traces means the traces left by various tools, usually the traces left when burglaries were committed, traces on windows or doors. And then this identification was called identifying signs on certain items. Usually vehicles were stolen, so we would investigate the traces left on vehicles. Then there were traces on various kinds of locks, safe locks or ordinary locks. The purpose was to determine how these locks had been picked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to your work in the field of mechanical traces, did you become involved in any other work? Did you become involved in analysing traces of another kind? And if so, could you tell us which field -- which other field you started working in.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Later on I became specialised in investigating traces left by firearms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, could you tell me how many individuals worked in the forensics department, which is where you, too, worked. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993 -- in 1992 and 1993, since there are a lot of workers who were coming and going because of the conditions that prevailed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the number of workers fluctuated, but there were always at least ten employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what sort of qualifications did these people have, these people who worked in the forensics department? What sort of professional level did they have?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: All the employees in the forensics department had a basic form of training at least. And some of the employees had also specialised in certain fields.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, in which fields did you have experts and what did they specialise in?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I'll -- Djaferovic Izet was the chief, the head of the department. In addition to his basic training, he had specialised in dactyloscopics and graphology. Dactyloscopics in English would be fingerprints.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The interpretation was not correct. The witness pointed out that the word "dactyloscopija" was not interpreted correctly. Obviously the witness can understand English.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: No, but I know it should be "fingerprints" in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, Mr. Dzaferovic, apart from having basic training in forensics had specialised in the field you have just mentioned. In which other fields were there employees who had specialist knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic Redzo, apart from having basic forensics training, he had specialised knowledge, too. Hadzic, Redzo. He had specialised -- he was a professor of biology and chemistry. He had specialised in biological chemical traces and in fingerprinting, too. As far as Redzo Hadzic is concerned, he was the most senior employee we had. He also founded a collection for the CSB. And maybe I should tell you what this monocollection is. I should clarify this. It's a collection of individual fingerprints of individuals who had been processed, that is to say the fingerprints of individuals who had committed crimes at the time. I had specialised in mechanical traces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, which area was the CSB active in, or rather, where did your forensics department carry out analysis in the fields that you covered?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The CSB operated in the area along the Bosna River, Davidovici, Zepce, Zenica, Kakanj; and in the Lasva valley, Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Bugojno, Donji and Gornji Vakuf. And in that same area, the forensics department carried out its work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the police administrations of these various places that you have just mentioned, did you have forensics departments or did you have other individuals who could carry out some of the investigations that were required to establish certain facts?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: In public security stations, we didn't have forensic departments, we just had forensic technicians who would process crimes within the terms of reference of the basic courts. That was the most frequent situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Husejnagic, on whose instructions and how were crime experts or forensic equipment used and engaged?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The most frequent situation was through the operations officer in the security services centre who would, after having been informed about a particular event, form depending on the kind of offence an investigating team. So depending on the type of act, for instance whether it's manslaughter, theft, or the like, a particular number of specialists would be engaged for the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war and during 1992 and 1993, what kind of equipment did the forensic department have available to it at the Zenica CSB?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The forensic equipment of CSB Zenica was quite appropriate and it had all the necessary equipment and material for carrying out all investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those resources and equipment in those days, that is the beginning of 1993, were they also available to the military police of the 3rd Corps that was situated in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: In view of the specific nature of these resources which are part of the forensic department, the forensic experts of the military could not have the same kind of resources and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, what could they have had at the beginning of 1993 to be able to do their work?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Apart for photographic equipment, the rest such as dactiloscopic equipment or any other equipment, that is equipment for fingerprint analysis, could not be obtained in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of this, tell me please: Was there any cooperation in 1993 between the military police of the 3rd Corps and the CSB, and was your forensic equipment used for certain investigative activities when these were done by military personnel? Do you know whether any such cooperation was established?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Very frequently -- most frequently employees from the forensic department would assist the military police, mainly due to the specific resources that were required and the specific expertise of the experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Husejnagic, when this investigating team is formed, depending on the type of offence and when it does its on-site inspection for the serious crimes for which you are equipped, who is in charge of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge is in charge of the investigation. He is the head of the investigating team.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who issues assignments to your employees, that is to your specialists on site? Who gives instructions as to the kind of investigative procedures that the CSB will engage in when you do your on-site inspection?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The head of the investigating team, which means the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once you have completed your part of the job, that is you do what you have been instructed to do by the investigating judge, who do you submit your findings to?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: We would submit our findings to the court that this judge comes from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, at some point in time to the best of your recollection, that is in January 1993, did your forensic department and inspectors of the security services, were they requested to do some analysis in connection with the death of certain persons from Dusina whose bodies were brought to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, were you part of that team that did the on-site inspection?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of that team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small point of interpretation. In your language you put the question to the witness: The death or the murder, because in the French interpretation we heard "murder" or "assassination." What was your question in your language? In English it is death and in French it is murder. I don't know if it's going directly from the B/C/S or through the English. So could you please ask the witness the question again. Just a moment, please. The Prosecution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there is a similar issue. Perhaps it's an interpretation issue. The witness was asked about an on-site inspection, and if he could clarify -- it's the first time we hear that, that there was an on-site inspection. That's obviously an important issue. What does that mean? Was that the team which was pulled together? That's called the on-site inspection team, or did they in fact go to the crime scene? I'm just not sure how this term comes into play, because that's not what the witness said. It was formulated as a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, could you please ask the witness to clarify so that the translation in all three languages corresponds.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, let me cut up my previous question into several simpler questions. So please answer them for me. At any point in time were you a member of the investigating team which was asked to do some examinations at the morgue in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of those examinations that were carried out at the morgue in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The judge of the military court, Mr. Mirsad Strika was in charge and another judge of the military court was present Vlado Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you're going to the place, that is to the morgue of the hospital in Zenica. Was it connected to the arrival of the bodies of persons who had been killed in the village of Dusina and who had been transported to the hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was linked to that, to what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that everything has been clearly interpreted, because in answer to your question I never spoke about murder; I spoke about persons who were killed. So in our language, "killing" is death that occurs in battle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In French the word is "tuer," in English, "killed." Perhaps the most precise term would be persons who died. Because in "killed" there is a connotation of murder. So you have the choice: Died, killed, or assassinated. So it is up to you to use the most appropriate term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I be more precise?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do, but I think in word -- in the war we use "killed."

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: In the police jargon we use the words nastradali, which means those who suffered death.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think the Judge has given us some instructions now and we will bear this in mind to make sure that the word we use can be adequately interpreted into other languages. Thank you. You have just given us the name of the investigating judge and of another judge of the district military court who were present. I'm not sure the names came out clearly. Could you repeat who was the head of the team among the judges and which judge of the district military court was also present.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I said a judge of the military court was in charge and his name is Mirsad Strika. And also present for a part of those activities was another judge from the military court, Vlado Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who gave you specific assignments with respect to this particular case as to the steps you need to take?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Judge Strika Mirsad.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to show the witness, with the help of the usher, Your Honour, a few documents. These are documents that we showed earlier on. There's only one new document. We have a sufficient number of copies for Your Honours and for my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to look at the document number 1. It is document P332, Exhibit P332. Would you please tell me whether this is a document of the security services in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The initials in the lower-left corner, "SCSA," are the initials of the person who actually drafted the document, but the chief of the centre signed it. "SE" stands for the initials of one of the employees of the CSB who was present during those activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Husejnagic, is this the standard format of a document whereby the CSB submits findings to the court after having carried instructions of the court [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: As the military court had requested certain investigations to be done this was the most customary way in which these documents would be submitted to the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of this document we see attachments and annexes, and four are listed. Tell me, the annexes listed in this document, are they the reports of authorised bodies compiled by them upon the request of the court or are they something else? At the bottom of the document, we just see the word "annexes."

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could perhaps through the signatures identify the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will come to those documents later. But in connection with this particular document, is it customary to forward as annexes the results of the investigations that you conducted, be they forensic or other analyses?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The annexes reflect the activities that we engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the bottom it says "photo record." Tell me, who photographed the persons in the morgue in Zenica? Who prepared the photo documents in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: In this particular case I took the photographs of all the ten victims and bodies and I think that -- those documents should bear my signature. And as we worked as a team, there should be the signature also of Hadzic Redzo, another employee of our department.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Husejnagic, were those photographs in colour or black and white?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: These were black and white photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you now look at the document number 2. This is Prosecution Exhibit 334 [as interpreted]. Do you know the person who compiled this note? Sorry, 333. In line 24, there's an error in the exhibit number. The exhibit number is 333.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I do know. Should I answer your question? I know the person since 1991. That is when I started working in the CSB up until last year. Last year, this person passed away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was Redzo Hadzic was also present during this examination in the hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Redzo Hadzic and myself did most of the work involved in this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You wanted to say something before I put my question to you. I interrupted you. If there is anything you would like to add, please add it.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: As far as Redzo Hadzic is concerned when I was at the forensic department, I was his boss. That's why I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at document number 3, please. The document number, the exhibit number is P334. Do you know the person who compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, from before 1991. And to this day I can even recognise the signature because even today I am this person's boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, is that the same person whose initials you recognised in the attached document and you said that this person had probably drafted the attached document?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the person whose initials are "ES" for Enes Saric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Enes Saric also at the site where some of the investigation was carried out under the supervision of Judge Strika?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Enes was involved in that work. He was an inspector, or rather we called these duties the duties of an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document number 5 now -- I apologise, under number 4. Could you tell me whose signature you can see here. Do you know these persons?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Expert analysis performed by Redzo Hadzic and then there is the person I have already identified, Enes Saric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, although you have already spoken about specialists in your forensics department, could you tell me whether Redzo Hadzic had any specialist knowledge in order to examine chemical and other traces.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Redzo Hadzic was a professor of chemistry and biology. And in addition to the basic training he had, he had also specialised in biological and chemical traces and in fingerprinting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at page number 1. Have a look at the last sentence in the B/C/S version of the analysis. It says that it was requested that it be established whether there were particles of gun powder in the paraffin samples that were sent. Can you find that sentence?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A specialist in the CSB who gave you this task, who made this request?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The judge from the military court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at page 2 of this analysis. And in the middle of the second paragraph it says that the reaction in the paraffin test --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The name of the judge doesn't appear in line 20, page 30. The witness mentioned the name. He said it was Strika Mirsad, the judge of the district military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. In the second paragraph on the second page you can see something that concerns the corpse of Pero Ljubicic. And here one sees that the reaction on both -- the reaction of the paraffin test on both hands of Ljubicic Pero was negative. Since you were involved in the duties you have mentioned in the course of the war in the CSB, I want to know if you have any knowledge that in the course of combat civilians were killed, too.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you had carried out the tasks you were ordered to carry out by the investigating judge, who would you forward your reports to?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: We would forward our reports to the court, to the courts where the judge who had issued the order worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you personally, together with Redzo Hadzic, carried out most of the work in the course of that analysis, and you said that you took the photographs yourself. Tell me whether the photographs you took reflected the wounds on the bodies that you photographed.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these photographs, did anyone else examine and describe the wounds on those bodies?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was done by a pathologist, Dr. Faruk Turkic. He was a pathologist who worked in the Zenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the work that you did, do you know whether the pathologist Dr. Turkic had specialist knowledge and was experienced in such work?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: At the time he was the only doctor who worked for the high court or the military court. He was the only doctor who did such work. And I think that he was quite experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether Dr. Turkic was also present when the investigating judge was carrying out his work in the Zenica hospital morgue.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was present. We were all present, all those so far mentioned were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now have a look at document number 5. Mr. Husejnagic, could you tell me drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Dr. Faruk Turkic compiled this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who issued an order requesting that Mr. Turkic carry out this specialist work?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The Judge Mirsad Strika did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To whom did the pathologist have to submit his report on the analysis, carried out in accordance with the order issued by the judge?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, as in our case, to the institution where the judge worked, and that was the Zenica military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, since you were at the site, you were in the hospital where you performed some of your duties and you took photographs of all the bodies, tell me whether you were able to determine -- whether you were able to notice the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: A forensics expert could provide you with the best answer, but obviously it was a result of gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When examining them and taking the photographs, or rather later when developing the photographs did you notice anything on those bodies that was different from the sort of wounds that the bodies of those killed in the course of combat usually had?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just an observation. This person here, the witness, is obviously the head of the forensic department. And we've heard his credential as a -- I think he had an engineering degree in mechanics. I'm really not sure whether he had talk about the causes of death and how it relates to other bodies, since he didn't -- clearly didn't perform any autopsies on these bodies. So I would object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, given the time which you examined [as interpreted] and photographed the bodies of these individuals, were you able to notice any differences between the wounds that these bodies had and the wounds that you would see when you examined the bodies of other individuals who had been killed in the course of combat?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: My answer would be similar to the previous one. A forensics expert would be in the best position to answer your question. But given the knowledge that I had, I didn't notice anything that might indicate that they had died as a result of being tortured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, in the course of 1993, were you ever in a position to see other bodies that had been brought in from areas where there had been fighting?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, even in the course of 1992 I was present during investigations of quite serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you saw such corpses that had been brought in from areas where there was fighting, tell me whether on the basis of what you could see those bodies had wounds -- gunshot wounds that were similar to the wounds that the bodies that you saw in the Zenica hospital morgue had.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the wounds were similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look on page 6 in the B/C/S version of the document drafted by Dr. Turkic. Have a look at the general conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under item 2 it says that the entry wounds were inflicted by fairly powerful weapons from a distance of more than 1 metre. Tell me, when it says that the wounds were inflicted from a distance of over 1 metre, why is it necessary for this to be stated in such a finding and what does it mean, since later on you also specialised in the field of firearms?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, this statement was included because in the area around the entry wounds no gunpowder particles were found. The traces of gunpowder weren't found around the wounds on these corpses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Husejnagic, is: When you photographed the bodies, were you able to find traces of gunpowder particles on the photographs that you developed?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, I wasn't able to find such traces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Husejnagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have now concluded my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is now 10.35. We will have our break and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has completed their examination-in-chief. The other Defence team, do they have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I shall give the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Husejnagic.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you. It shouldn't take too long. Let me go first to this paraffin test, as it's called. And you were asked a few questions about this test, or rather the result. And this Exhibit P341, which is in the bundle you have received number 4. We don't need the document. I just want to ask you: You personally conducted this paraffin test?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't do that analysis. The document is signed by my colleague at the time, Redzo Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it was him who conducted it?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the --

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could specify. Part of the preparatory duties I was involved in, that is taking the paraffin tests. But the analysis of the tests, the results, was done by the signatory of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the technique of the paraffin test?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions in relation to that. So the way I understand the test, you are looking, or the person who conducts the test looks whether there are traces of firearms or gunpowder on the skin or clothes of a body. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The way to conduct this test, the way I understand you, but please correct me, is you are looking for traces, for residual elements of gunpowder on the skin or the surface of a body. That's the starting point for this test?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: In the case of paraffin tests, we are looking for gunpowder particle traces on the hands, on the hands of certain persons, depending on the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that would mean, then, if you find any such traces that the person has fired a firearm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: One cannot be 100 per cent explicit about it. There may be a certain contact with a firearm, something close to a firearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that would also leave these traces?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand. After what? Once you do the paraffin test, there should be no traces left where the paraffin test was done, if that is what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not exactly. You said that traces are left either if somebody has shot a firearm; or second, and that's a clarification by you, if somebody came in certain contact with a firearm, something close to a firearm. So in these two situations traces may be found on the hand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The task of the forensic expert is to analyse chemical traces. But I do have certain knowledge about it. So if necessary, I can provide a clarification. So in this case the question is: Who does this type of analysis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But let me just clarify what you told us before. When there are traces on somebody's hands, either this person has shot a firearm himself or he came -- and those are your words: "He came into certain contact with a firearm, something close to a firearm." So those are the two situations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I need to explain the process of firing a shot, and this is linked to ballistics, and that would need to be explained. What is the distance? What type of particles are left on the hands, how they are carried, et cetera. But this is the duty of a forensic expert for chemical traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. That won't be necessary. Let me ask you, if somebody shot a firearm, so obviously there may be some traces on his hand, and later within an hour he surrendered, was captured, and executed, if you then find the bodies and examine the bodies, there may still be traces on the hands of this person because he has fired a firearm before he was captured. Is that a fair assessment, what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The answer would be similar to my previous answer. The question should be put to the person carrying out the analysis. The only possibility would be for me as a -- I don't know, if I was here in the capacity of a forensic expert then I might be able to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you a different question. For how long do the traces remain on the hands after a person fired a -- fired a gun or got into contact. How long thereafter the firing are you as a specialist able to determine: Yes, we do a chemical test; yes, there are traces?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It depends on a number of factors, but again, this is a question that is identical to the previous one. I am a forensic expert for mechanical traces and ballistics, currently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the bodies you have examined, you were part of that team pursuing these paraffin tests. The date you examined it was the 28th of January or the 29th of January. If you look at P341. Again, this is your number 4. Can you tell us again the date this test was conducted.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of January were the following acts done: Photographs were taken of all ten bodies, paraffin tests, and index fingerprints of some persons who could not be identified by persons who were doing the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you're saying the 28th. But if you look at just a document I referred you to, "Date 29 January, 1993. Subject: Re: Paraffin test, expert analysis." It starts on 29th January, 1993. "Ten unknown bodies brought from Dusina, Lasva," and so on, and so on. Perhaps you don't recall, but here it seems to indicate that the tests were conducted on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: We have to distinguish two stages: The paraffin test itself and an analysis of the paraffin test. The paraffin test was done on the 28th of January. And an analysis of those paraffin tests, or paraffin gloves, as we call them -- perhaps I could explain the procedure to make it quite clear to everyone, but again this is rather specific. The analysis was done on the 29th. The test was carried out on the 28th of January and then the analysis of the results was done the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where were these tests carried out on the 28th? What was the location? Was it also the morgue at the Zenica hospital or was it at a different place?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: No. In the laboratory of the MUP, that is the centre of security services Zenica, in the chemical laboratory of that centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you present when the bodies were brought in?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: No. I was probably at my workplace in the security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were not present on the 28th when these bodies were brought in.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present in the morgue of the hospital. I was present in Zenica. I think I was at my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Anyway, do you know when the -- these persons, these ten persons, deceased? Do you know the date?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that the doctor made a rough assessment of that date, but that was part of his assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I tell you that the date was 26th of January that these people deceased, can you now help us: If the paraffin test or the analysis was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. done two days later how long the traces would still be discoverable?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: This time I will answer the question. If somebody is killed, traces of gunpowder particles remain on the hands for quite a long time, on condition that the body is not bathed or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you asked the expert can he quantify, what does he mean: "Quite a long time"? Three days? A week? Perhaps longer? Perhaps less?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Again this is part of chemical analysis. The gunpowder particles that are found are quite resilient. The problem is to what extent they will be preserved. The duration is up to the chemist. Most of these products nitrates and -- nitrates are preserved for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You're leaving it up into the air. Obviously, after two days they were still visible. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. And coming back to my earlier point, you cannot really say whether the persons subject of these paraffin test who had positive tests were not later, perhaps an hour, two, three, captured and later executed. You cannot exclude that from a finding of a positive paraffin test.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It's not up to me to make such an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave the paraffin test and let's talk about the crime-scene investigation. I take it that during the war - and I'm talking after you finished your education which was I understand stopped on the 4th of April in Vrace in Sarajevo - did you conduct a lot of investigations into violent deaths during the war period, let's say until the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: An innumerable number of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you go to the actual crime scene, the site, and look at where the bodies, if there are bodies, are lying; look at the distances; look at the location and perhaps make sketches? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: No, we did not go on site because these happened in the area of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But there must have been situations - just any situation, I'm not talking about something specific - where you went to a crime scene and investigated like policemen do. Are you telling us there was not a single instance you went to a crime scene and conducted on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I said that I conducted any number of investigations, but not in the area of war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to show a witness a document which we have found in the last couple of days as part of our searches. And it goes only to the credibility of this witness of his previous answer. And unfortunately, I only gave it to the Defence just before the break because I thought it wasn't possible. But I would like to show him the document and I have sufficient copies I believe for Your Honours. And perhaps the witness can tell us what this document is all about, because it appears to contradict of what he just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor to the Defence. According to our decision regarding documents that are produced after the closing of the Prosecution case, the Prosecution can produce documents only on two grounds. First, the credibility or to refresh the memory of the witness. So you're telling us you have a document which would allow you to check the credibility of the witness. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, pursuant to your decision, we of course have no objection if the Prosecution has a document that could challenge the credibility of this witness. However, the Prosecution during the last break gave us a document which, according to what the witness had just said, that he had attended any number of on-site investigations, cannot contradict his statement. I think the Prosecution has not laid the grounds for showing this document. So I think this is not one of the cases you specified in your ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, with Your Honour's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question of credibility relates to which particular point? Because the Defence is telling us the witness has said that he didn't do crime-scene inspections. Do you have a document showing that he did? To what particular does your document refer when it comes to credibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. He said -- the witness that he did not conduct on-site investigations because of a war situation. And we have here a document, it's a short one, which is titled: Sketch of the crime scene, and it relates to the recovery of 27 dead bodies. And the witness -- it dates 15th September, 1995. And it shows in detail what the witness did, that he went to the crime scene; that he took very, very detailed sketches. Perhaps he forgot about it. I would just like to show him the document and ask his comment about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. I'll give you the floor. You're telling us that you have a document, I see in the English transcript, which is dated the 15th of September, 1995. That is what the English transcript says, the 15th of September. And there's a drawing of 27 bodies. And does this relate to the on-site inspection for these persons that we're talking about or is it another on-site inspection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's another on-site inspection, something that the witness has denied that he did. That's why I would like to show him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you look at page 41, line 20, the witness said: I was -- "attended an innumerable number" of investigations, but did not carry out on-site inspections in combat areas. Therefore, a document from 1995 can be covered by these innumerable on-site inspections that he has referred to, so I don't see how it contradicts that he had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the witness said, as you yourself say on page 41, that he didn't go on site. But we have a document showing the opposite, apparently. Mr. Usher, before showing the document, the Judges wish to have a look at it. Show this document to the witness and we'll see what he can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As you heard, Mr. Husejnagic, this is a document. You'll see it because it appears that you signed it dated from 15th September, 1995. And it's a location Oborci in Donji Vakuf. And perhaps you can tell us how it came about that you made these very detailed drawings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is the English translation. I don't think he needs to say that. And, yes, that's the first page of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps if you can tell us the title, what it says, in your language.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The drawing of the on-site finding. This is a document that I compiled, but this is an investigation that took place on the 15th of September, 1995, after the cessation of hostilities in that area. I may add, this particular case, we had here 27 captured persons from the area of Kljuc, I think they were, who had been killed near the elementary school in Oborci near Donji Vakuf. And the investigation was done on the 15th of September when there were no combat operations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you did? Did you -- is that the actual scene where people were deceased? Because I see rifle bullets, and so on, by a dead body. Was that the area which you believe was the crime scene were these people were killed?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to this event of the 15th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Did you find all these bullets on the ground by these various bodies, as listed on page 2?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter of bullets. Under 1 there was a group of 77 cartridges, a group of cartridges. And there were seven 8.62 times 39 cartridges. And there were four bullets and the cartridges were of the calibre that I have mentioned. I think everything is clear here. I don't know what else I could clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these bullets you found by the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The cartridges, on the whole, they are cartridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. You found those by the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, why did you go there, to this scene?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we were obeying the order issued by the judge. Idriz Katkic, I think that's his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you go to the last page of this document, just the last page. Did you make this drawing yourself?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I think that I was helped by a forensics expert from Donji Vakuf, Bagori Casim [phoen] as far as I can remember, but this is another event. This is an on-site investigation after the cessation of hostilities. If we compare this to this case -- well, at the time we were carrying out investigations, some of the investigations, in the morgue of the Zenica hospital. But we didn't go to the site. This was ordered by military judges. And in 1995 I think the judge was Idriz Katkic. And in 1993 I think the judge was Mirsad Strika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just going back to this last page, I just see these four bodies lying there. Am I correct? These signatures, four bodies, two in the middle of the road and two other ones north-east of the first two bodies. Am I reading it correct?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what do these numbers mean? If you look at the body most north, 37/95, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: That's the number of the person who was killed. And he is recorded in a list of unidentified bodies. This list was compiled by the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know when these people were killed or deceased, these four people we see the drawings of?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: This relates to the 28 of them, not just to these four bodies. We found them at that site after the cessation of hostilities, but I don't know when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for helping me on this document. Now, let me go back to what you just told us a moment ago. I believe you said that you did not go to Dusina, arguably the scene of these events in January 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't go. That's correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You as an investigator or as a crime-scene specialist, would you have liked to go to Dusina to see what the real causes of these deaths were, the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: As far as the fighting is concerned -- well, when there was fighting we only worked when we received orders from judges from military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you personally --

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: So I as a specialist couldn't act independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I believe you may have answered that before to questions from the Presiding Judge. You were never interviewed in relation to by a judge or by another policeman in relation to these events at Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The tasks that I had, the tasks that my department performs now, well we were involved in the technical aspect of the work: recording traces; making sketches such as the one we have before us; taking photographs; finding fingerprints and other traces, on the basis of which light is shed on the event. But that aspect has to do with the work of an inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you aware that anybody from your department or from somewhere else did go to Dusina and make this nice drawing you have discussed a moment ago? Are you aware of any such crime-scene sketch being done in relation to Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: No one from my department did that, but there is nothing else that I know about it. As I have already said, because of the fighting we did not go to the scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was fighting in Dusina at the time you became involved into the -- these investigations into the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say now. Perhaps we would have gone there, but the judges were afraid. They were against us going. And we couldn't go without the judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which judge was afraid? Can you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in that specific case the judge was Mirsad Strika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he told you he was afraid to go -- or that you went to Dusina. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, Ermin Husejnagic couldn't decide on such matters. Someone assesses security here too, you know. Perhaps you don't and perhaps others don't. I don't know if that's clear or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But he told you he was afraid?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, he was responsible for issuing such orders. For the sake of security, for the sake of his safety and our safety, I assume he took the decision he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you about these photo documentations. I believe you said you personally photographed the bodies, the ten bodies, in black and white. And is it true that you put together a documentation containing these photographs?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I think so. Yes, that's certain. If you show me something like the text you showed me a minute ago, I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know where the original is of this photo documentation?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I know we handed it over to the military court, but right now I don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where are they normally kept after a case is finished or shelved? Where are these original documents usually kept?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a military court case, so the original documents should be sought via those channels. Or perhaps other bodies had received this material apart from the military court. But after the cessation of hostilities, I don't know where those documents were forwarded to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go to the last issue, that's document number 5 in your bundle. It hasn't been assigned yet a number. If you can have a look at document number 5. It is a report titled: External description of the bodies from Lasva near Zenica, if I have the right translation. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you help us? The bodies, the way they are described, it doesn't really say the names of these bodies. Can you help us and perhaps you can relate to the other documents in your bundle numbered 1, 2, 4. Which, for instance, is body number 1 in parenthesis or slash marked 2? Can you give us the name of this body? Perhaps document number 3 or document number 4 may help you.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: 1 through 93. Document number P334.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: 1/1993 [as interpreted], this number means that it's the unidentified body. 1 through 1993. This body was registered in the body of the CSB in 1993. It was registered as unidentified. And this body must have the same number on the photo record. Perhaps what the doctor said when it says marked 2. This is 2 through 93. This means 2 through 93, and that would be Voja Stanisic. I'm referring to document P334. That's how I found the name. And I'm looking at document number 5 compiled by this doctor, body number 1. But there was a 2 placed by the photograph. I think the photograph started with number 2, which is why this is how everything has been presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It's a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... summarise what I understand you are saying. So the first body as described by the doctor, in the report of the Dr. Turkic, the first body would be, and that's a cross-reference to document P334, would be Vinko Kegelj?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: No. 2 through 93, that's what I said. 2, it's marked "2." That's the number that we use in the register of unidentified bodies, which I referred to a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: 1 through 93, 1/93, if we have a look at the doctor's document, body 1. This is on page 5 of the doctor's document, body number 9. Is that clear now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So the name of body number 9 on the document would be whom, if you give him a name, body number 9?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It would be Vinko, son of Matija. Vinko, son of Matija, from Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that would be Vinko Kegelj ?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear. I don't know anyone here. All I know is how this is recorded. And it's on the basis of the way that this was recorded that I have provided you with these clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not entirely sure whether I'm clear. Tell us, looking at the report of Dr. Turkic the first body he discusses is called body number 1, marked number 2. What's the name of this body, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Stanisic, Vojo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the second body, number 2, marked 3. Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: 3/93, Pero Ljubicic. I'm referring to document P334 now. 1 through 93, 2 through 93, 3 through 93; these are the numbers we placed by the bodies when photographing them. And this is how the bodies were identified, but the doctor followed an order of his own and he recorded them under numbers of his own as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. I understand now. Let's continue it step by step. The third body in the doctor's report on page 2, it's called body number 3, marked 4. That would be?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Franjo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And body number 4, marked number 5 would be?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Augustin Rados.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Body number 5, marked 6 would be?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Stipo Kegelj, son of Mato.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Body number 6, marked 7?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: 7/93, Zvonko Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Then body number 7, marked 8?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: This document -- in the last paragraph of this document it says that body 8/93, it says that the above-named citizens were unable to identify the body, but they provided names of people who went missing from the Dusina area, namely Pero Rajic, son of Marko, and Mladen Kegelj, son of Jozo. I remember that we took the fingerprints of this person's right index finger. And when making a comparison, when comparing this fingerprint that was taken from body 8/93, when we compared this fingerprint with the fingerprints we had in the database of the police station in Zenica, it was determined that the person in question was Mladen Kegelj. This is in document P333.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph of that document it says: "Body number 8 was identified on the basis of the right index fingerprint. The body is that of Mladenko Kegelj, born on such-and-such a date in Dusina."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And body number 9 marked number 1 would be whom?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Vinko Kegelj, son of Mato 1 through 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last body, body number 10?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: 10/93, Drazen Kegelj, Drazenko Kegelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Now, were the bodies opened by the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The doctor didn't open the bodies. The doctor performed an external examination of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how long did he take to externally examine all these ten bodies, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember whether any bullets, any bullets, were found and indeed collected, noted somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any bullets being found. You mean bullets, don't you, parts of the bullets? If we had found anything, this would probably have been recorded in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the fact that it's not recorded, at least I don't see it, means that he did not find any bullets?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, these bodies were brought to the morgue from the scene. At the time it wasn't the cantonal hospital in Zenica. At the time there was no cantonal hospital. So the cartridges or the bullets that caused their death couldn't have been brought with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, looking at these ten bodies, I don't know whether you remember, do you remember whether they had wounds on their backs, entry wounds, on their backs?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The forensic expert in medicine should have made such an assessment, because - how should I put this? - the way in which this is determined is quite specific. So an expert in forensic medicine would be in a position to provide you with precise information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, earlier on you were asked a question -- to compare different types of casualties and perhaps you have acquired certain experience. If you don't know, it doesn't matter. But let me just refer you to the first body on Dr. Turkic's report. It's on the first page, and it's the last paragraph of the descriptions of body number 1. So please go to your bundle, number 5. It's the first page -- yes, that's the page. Body number 1, marked number 2. Just go down perhaps 15 lines. And in your version, there -- it -- five lines before the end of the discussion of body number 1. It says, and I quote: "There are five entry wounds -- entry wound openings in the region of the right scapula and at the back of the right upper arm. There are five exit wounds on the right front side of the thorax and on the right upper arm." Now, my question to you is: From your experience, these five entry wound openings in the region of the right scapula, can you assist us what the scapula means and its technical -- don't worry if you don't know. Perhaps you remember having seen the body, having seen the entry wounds. Do you know what scapula means?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Usually you refer to the chest, the left and the right part. So reference is being made to the rib cage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, the chest, usually that's thorax. So scapula would be, in medical terms, the shoulder blade, just to tell you that. Have you heard of that, scapula being the shoulder blade?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: These are medical terms, front and back side. There are expressions when we used about the chest from the front and the behind. After all, these are medical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So do you recall the body -- this first body number 1, that it had entry wounds at the back shoulder blades, five entry wounds, and then it comes out at the thorax, that's basically the breast. It's a large area, can't be more specific. Do you recall that in relation to body number 1?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: After so many years, it's hard for me to remember with any precision. I can just make a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps -- you don't need to do that. Perhaps one body which may have sticked out is body number 4 and you told us that was Augustin Rados. If you can go to page number 2 and it's also in your version on page number 2 the towards the end. But in fact in the English version what I want to talk about is the last paragraph. And in your version it's on page number 3, the top of page number 3, Mr. Husejnagic.
