Let me quote: "This body, Augustin Rados, there are 17 entry wounds inflicted by firearms on the front side of the thorax and on the abdomen. On the back, there are eight exit and three entry wounds in the region of the right scapula." Do you remember a body that's been so riddled by bullets from both sides? Do you remember this specific body?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Not with precision. I have a hazy remembrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this hazy remembrance. What did you see? How did the body look like?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Unless I could look at some documents, I'm unable to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, the documents you have in front of you, that's all we have today. Does it jog your memory, any of the documents? You can also read the whole paragraph of body number 4. It tells you -- he was, I guess, unusually tall. He was 196 centimetres tall and about 30 years of age.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you showed me another document with 28 victims. After so much time and after so many events, it's hard to remember anything well enough for me to be able to give you any concrete comments regarding the injuries and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Were you surprised to see, perhaps you and other people, that these people were shot from two sides or at least some of them were -- had entry wounds, both at the front and at the back? Did that surprise you, compared to other bodies you have seen in the course of that time?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It was no more unusual than the other events. Now, from these descriptions, it is obvious that automatic firearms were used. I could just give you an example. For example, the speed of firing of one type of such firearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these bodies were filmed, the dead bodies as appeared, naked bodies? Do you remember that they were filmed?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: We didn't do that part of the work, nor did I see anyone filming the bodies with a video camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it normal practice to film the bodies, or would that be something unusual in your experience?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The CSB in Zenica in those days did not have a video camera, at least my department didn't have one. Maybe somebody might have had it in private possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just ask you another small subject. Before you testified, the Defence informed us in a brief note of what you were going to talk about. And it says that families were notified in relation to, I take it, these bodies. Were you involved in identification of the families of the persons we discussed?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: That part of the work was done by the inspector of the CSB, Enes Saric, together with the judge. I assumed the judge, Iset Strika -- sorry, Mirsad Strika was also involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know when that was done?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of January. That was on that day. Now, whether some additional things were done the following day, I don't know. But I think that they managed to have almost all of the ten bodies identified on that day. I know there was talk that there was need to go to the morgue once again to examine the bodies. I don't know, therefore, whether a part of the work was left for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether these persons who contacted the family members, Mr. Saric or perhaps the judge, whether they had to travel to see these family members to inform them?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. As far as I know, they came themselves. They came of their own accord. Somebody from the army was present, representatives of the HVO, and some other citizens. And the judge, Vlado Adamovic would drop in, too. Now, what was the reason for this, I'm not sure. Maybe he did part of that work; I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Husejnagic. I appreciate your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Husejnagic, you were shown a document that you drafted in 1995 in the area of Donji Vakuf. Tell me, please, from 1992 until about the middle of 1995, who controlled Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I know that we did on-site inspections as the CSB when explosives were placed on the bridge at Donji Vakuf. After that inspection, we no longer had access to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the Army of Republika Srpska there?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that event. I don't know exactly when this on-site inspection was done, but I know that my boss at the time, Judge Izet did the inspection. And after that the Army of Republika Srpska would not allow access to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering questions from my learned friend you said you went to the crime scene after the cessation of hostilities. During that inspection, was Donji Vakuf liberated once again and placed under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We may have been maybe the third team that entered that area, after the Army of Republika Srpska had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering a question from my learned friend you said that you attended a large number of on-site inspections during the war. Was this one of the ones that you attended?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told your colleague that with respect to that event I made the sketches of the crime scene, and I think I also took photographs of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also told my learned colleague on page 41, line 20, that you didn't do on-site inspections in areas of combat operations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to carry out this on-site inspection in liberated Donji Vakuf, there was no fighting in Donji Vakuf at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was no combat. Now, exactly where the separation lines were just then, I don't know. But they were quite removed from the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you went to carry out this on-site inspection, the bodies that you drew were on the spot where you found them, or had they been already moved from another location?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: As far as we knew, and judging by the traces that we found on the crime scene and our conclusions, they were on the very spot where the injuries were inflicted as a result of which they passed away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the case that is before this Trial Chamber, the bodies you took photographs of and did other activities together with your colleagues with respect to them, where were those bodies when you were assigned the task to do these tests?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Those bodies had already been brought to the morgue. This is a separate section of the pathology ward where Dr. Faruk Turkic, the pathologist, works.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, as part of your overall activities in the CSB, were you ever aware of a case when the judge inspecting bodies brought to a place which is quite some distance from the crime scene, would he give instructions for those bodies to be taken back and placed on the spot where they died?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: This never occurred in my career.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So these two cases are quite different, because in that case the bodies were on the scene; and in this case the bodies were in hospital.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also you started answering a question from my learned colleague when he mentioned that one body was hit by 17 rounds. You said that the conclusion to be drawn was that an automatic weapon had been used. Tell Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. me, what is the speed with this an automatic rifle can fire a burst of fire, a large number of bullets?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Depending on the type of automatic weapon, a Kalashnikov was frequently used and it can fire 150 rounds per minute. A light machine-gun, M-84, 1.000 rounds a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question you answered, saying that Judge Katkic had given you instructions to carry out certain activities in Donji Vakuf. And Judge Strika, instructions with respect to the bodies from Dusina. Tell me, as specialists, can you act contrary to or without a decision of the investigating judge who is in charge of these -- this part of the procedure?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I've already answered that question. We cannot be independent in our work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has some questions for you, and specifically I would like to show you a video which was admitted into evidence. So, Mr. Registrar, would it be possible P718. Could we screen it? It has already been shown. The Prosecution produced this. It is V000-2400.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we can assist. It should be running from our system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We are ready to play it, Your Honours, if you want us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are now going to watch a videotape and you will comment on it. I'm showing you this video in view of the fact that you told us that you took part in the investigation into the deaths of certain persons, and this video shows the bodies. We will ask you for your comments. So could the Prosecution play the video through their system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we eliminate the sound? It would be better. No sound and no comments, just the pictures, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we stop now? Look at this picture closely. You see a body. Look at the neck. As a specialist and a forensic expert, the trace one sees on the neck, was it caused by a bullet or by some other means? What would you say to us as a specialist?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: A competent expert for body injuries is the medical forensic expert and this shot is not too clear. I can make a judgement arbitrarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the forensic medical expert described the bodies, were you present? Were you with the expert when he was describing the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I was present when these examinations were done. I did not assist the pathologist. He had his own assistant for that. I just took the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. But you were present. What I'm showing you on this neck, you must have seen it. It's visible.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Did I see it then? Now, I see it now. And I don't remember seeing it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I think at the time, no such traces were evident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us just now that you were -- that you had certain knowledge about bullets and projectiles. Can you confirm that you have some knowledge about gunfire. You have such knowledge or not? What are you telling us?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I do have knowledge. Are you referring to this specific event or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But with the knowledge you have, what one sees, could this have been caused by a bullet? This is an ultrasimple question I'm putting to you. Could this have been due to a bullet? Because we see a scar. Could it have been caused by a bullet? You said during your career you saw an X number of bodies, so I'm asking you a technical question. Can what we see have been caused by a bullet? If you don't know, say that you don't.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It's hard to be precise in such a situation simply on the basis of this fact, or rather this video picture that I am looking at. What I mean is I don't know how to put it, one needs to know the circumstances under which something is happening. One needs to have more precise factors on the basis of which to draw conclusions. I could sort of arbitrarily make a judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Stop the video, please. Continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to stop now and we'll continue with the questions after the break. It is 12.30 and we'll resume about 5 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. Check to see if the transcript is working; it is. Witness, you were shown a video just before we adjourned, and like everyone else in the courtroom, you watched the video. There were traces of wounds on these bodies the size of which was different. Could you explain how it is that the wounds on the bodies were of different sizes, the holes made were different sizes. Is there anything you could say, any explanation you could provide?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depends on what?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: It depends on the trajectory of the bullet, or rather, it depends on the obstacles encountered by the bullets. A bullet in the course of its trajectory can be deviated, the bullets can be affected -- so the bullets can be affected. As a rule in ballistics, entry wounds have a smaller diameter. It depends on whether the bullet was deformed. If that is the case, the exit wound can be of a bigger size.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that you were present when the pathologist examined the bodies. Were the corpses -- when the corpses were examined, were they completely naked?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you can remember when the bodies were examined, were there still traces of blood?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I assume that there were. It depended on the position of the body. As the bodies were turned around, blood would appear from certain parts of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have said that you had already attended such examinations. When somebody dies a violent death, at the time were autopsies performed or not? As a specialist, a technician, what would you say? Was it almost obligatory to perform autopsies when the cause of death was a violent one, or was this for the judges to decide? As a specialist, what is your position about this issue?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, only a judge can order an autopsy to be performed. That's the case for the current law on criminal procedure and for the former one. This event referred to by the Prosecutor -- well, as far as the event in 1995 is concerned, the event was similar to the one referred to by the Prosecutor. The examination of the victims was identical to the examination of the victims in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as far as you know, were there any cases in which complete autopsies were performed? Are there any cases that you yourself were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with many cases, many such cases. But on the whole these cases involved - well, how would I put it -- civilian part of the work, as far as combat is concerned when there was fighting, autopsies were rarely performed. So I'm telling what I know, on the basis of my experience. I know -- I'm familiar with these two events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Faruk Turkic, was he someone who was capable of performing an autopsy? Because in forensic medicine it's necessary to have diplomas in medicine and certain knowledge. Was this doctor capable of performing an autopsy, in accordance with the rules of forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Dr. Faruk Turkic was a pathologist. This means someone who determines the cause of death. As this to whether he had any knowledge in the field of forensic medicine, I don't know. But all I do know is at that time the only doctor who could carry out that work in that area was this person I have referred to. He was the most competent doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the body is examined, if one assumes that there were gunshot wounds, doesn't one try to find the bullets in the body?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This can be done when an autopsy is performed, and as I said an autopsy was not performed at the time. And in the case of similar events, autopsies weren't performed either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's go back to the document that Defence counsel showed you a while ago. And could you have a look at document number 4, P341, dated the 29th of January. It's the document on the paraffin test. Can you see the first page? On the first page it says that on the 29th of January -- maybe I'll translate this. "Bodies brought from Dusina, from Lasva, were identified and paraffin tests were performed on each body, et cetera. But I see that there was no paraffin test for the body of Stanisic. And in English it says that it was impossible to approach the body. Where was Stanisic's body? Do you have an explanation, because ten bodies are referred to and there are nine paraffin tests, yet there was no test performed on this body. How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, I would say that for technical reasons -- well, in the morgue there are only two tables and the room is about 4 by 5 metres. That's the area where the examinations were carried out. And given the number of bodies, since that's the only morgue and since there were many other bodies of people who had died in other ways, well I assumed that this was the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The paraffin test we were provided with a description under "findings." We were provided with a description of the test. I won't go into the technique -- the technical details, which is very simple if you're familiar with this procedure, but I have a minor question. When you take samples for the chemical reaction of defemalin [phoen], how do you proceed? How do you take samples from the hands to determine whether there's any nitrate, oxide, et cetera? How do you proceed? How do you take samples?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: We used the paraffin gloves to collect samples. The procedure is as follows, I should explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly. How do you proceed?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: You take paraffin that dissolves at a certain temperature and has a certain purity. It dissolves and then you put the paraffin on the hands. After it has solidified - after a certain period of time has passed, the time depends on the warmth of the body - you take the paraffin gloves off and then you perform an analysis of those paraffin gloves under microscope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case of Stanisic's body it wouldn't have taken long to perform that test. Why wasn't this test done? You say the body was there, but why?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember that body now. The body was photographed, but you know if you only have one table and then you move one body to one place and another to another place and the room is only 4 by 5 metres, I assume that as a result the workers who were carrying out the work simply left. This is just an assumption, but that might be the technical reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll go on to another question. Have a look at document 5. We have a description in that document of the bodies, an external description of the bodies. There are no names for these bodies. You have identified the names. You said number 1 was Mr. Stanic [as interpreted], you said 2 was Pero Ljubicic, et cetera. On the 28th of January, they were not identified. On the 29th of January we were identified, as we can see in document 334 and in document P341. We have the first and last names and the dates of birth. On the basis of documents and you are a specialist in fingerprints, fingerprints were taken -- fingerprints of their right index fingers were taken and then these fingerprints were then compared to fingerprints that the Zenica police station apparently had. As far as you can remember, is this what actually happened? How were the fingerprints compared?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, how would I put it? Comparisons made on -- in the files that relate to identity cards of all the individuals who lived in the state, in these files you have the fingerprints of these individuals' right index fingers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the identity cards were where? Where were these victims' identity cards, if they had them?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't see those documents on any of them. This was something that the inspector from the CSB was involved in, Saric Enes. We were involved in the technical part of the work, photographing, et cetera, in the paraffin test that I have spoken about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a look at document number 5 now which contains descriptions of the bodies. Could you have a look at the description of body number 7. It says that it's a male, 185 centimetres tall, about 30 years of age, et cetera. In line 4 it says: The face is extremely deformed and unrecognisable because of broken bones." Can you see that? Can you see that sentence? And then it says --

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Which document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document number 5, which provides an external description of the bodies. It's dated the 28th of January. And in this document, which was compiled by the pathologist who was following orders issued by the judge, Mirsad Strika, there are ten bodies that were examined. I would like you to have a look at body number 7, marked 8. Can you see that part? It's on page 3. The description commences as follows: "The body of a male, 185 centimetres tall, et cetera." Have a look at line 4 in this paragraph. I'll read line 4. I'll translate the English into French. It says: "The face is extremely deformed and unrecognisable because of broken bones." And it continues. It says that "the nose is also deformed; the mouth is open." When it says that the face is deformed, how is it that it doesn't say that it's deformed as a result of a gunshot wound? Because if a bullet was in question, how could one explain the fact that the face is extremely deformed? As a technician, what would you say? Is the deformation caused by a bullet or something else? Because in the paragraph that follows it says: "The face is deformed and it's difficult to recognise it because of the broken bones." What would your conclusion be?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: As far as wounds to the head are concerned, it means that a bone was encountered as an obstacle. If a bullet encounters a bone which is an obstacle, then this causes significant deformations. The exit wounds are frequently very ugly. So if there were two wounds inflicted to the head, then very frequently you have such cases. At this moment I can't really be precise, but this is a situation that occurred frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But given what you have said as far as the technical matters are concerned, how is it that the pathologist did not indicate, did not mention, that there was a bullet in the head? Because according to what you said, these deformations and these multiple fractures can only be the result of the bullet or of several bullets. How is it that this description does not mention the fact that there was a bullet? How would you explain this? Can you provide an explanation?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, look -- how would I explain that, What would I say? If an automatic firearm was used, a fast weapon, then it can even sever part of the body. For example, if it can fire a lot of bullets in a minute, then it can even sever part of the body, and this would occur. So there would no longer be an entry point or an exit point; all you could see would be a deformation. That is really the case with the head, because a bullet is immediately encountered. As far as soft tissue is concerned, the situation is a little different after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But wouldn't it have been possible to perform an autopsy to determine the trajectory of the bullet?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, regarding the trajectory of the bullet, we need to have two fixed points. No autopsy was done in this case. Whether there were two fixed points or not, I am unable to say now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You can't make any conclusions. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I have a few questions for you. The first one is the following. You mentioned the names of the judges at the investigation concerning the bodies we talked about. There was also a prosecutor present. Do you also remember his name or don't you?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the name. I know he doesn't have the most important role in those activities, so I don't remember the specific person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I have two other questions for you. One relates to what you've said one or two minutes ago, talking about wounds caused by gunshots. If you read the report that is number 5 in your set of documents, you see that the doctor very often says that there is a wound the size of a -- the palm of a man's hand or the palm of a child's hand. And it strikes me that in a number of situations in which he makes this remark, he also said that it is an exit wound. Is there a relationship between exit wounds and the size of wounds, as you suggested a minute ago? You said exit wounds caused terrible exit shots, exit -- an exiting bullet caused terrible wounds.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I said that depending on the obstacles that the bullet comes across, the round, what obstacle it comes against, it may depart from its trajectory. And then it carries with it the material it comes across. For instance, if it hits against bone, hard bone, the bone is fragile, brittle, and a kind of conical crater is formed. And that is why the exit wounds are ugly when the round encounters a hard obstacle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I think I understand what you are saying. When the doctor writes about wounds the size of the palm of a hand or a child's hand, he -- well, if he asks you -- if the doctor writes such things in his report, what would you see, as a layman, if you read there is a wound the size of a hand, the palm of a hand? What would you expect to see as a layman? Is there a hole or something else?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: The exit wound, as I explained a moment ago. The entry wound can be smaller and the exit wound larger, especially when the round encounters these obstacles. Not along the whole channel so as to make a hole. In my view, a hole is something that is hollow throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But my question was: If the doctor -- the doctor who made this report writes about a wound as large as the size of the palm of a man, the palm of a child's hand, would that correspond with what you are telling? Would -- may I expect as a reader to be confronted with a hole in that case? I'm just asking: What does he mean when he says that?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I think that he was trying to say entry and exit wound in a way, because he knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. He very often mentioned in this respect exit wounds but doesn't do it always. So is the question that he had in mind [indiscernible]. Two other questions I still have. One relates to a discussion between the Prosecutor and you. The Prosecutor said when somebody is shot from different angles, can this be a war situation and you said, yes, this can very well be caused in a war situation. Now, if you read the report of the doctor you see that in the case of three bodies, body 1, body 3, and body 10 in this list, there were only wounds -- entries of bullets at the back. So these people have died by bullets that only came from the back side. My question to you would be: Is that something that is quite normal in war situations, in a fight? Or is that exclusively a phenomenon that is not related to a fight?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: All kinds of things happen. One cannot make any conclusions solely based on that particular fact. The configuration of the land is very important. It could even be decisive when making conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: For instance, when they were in the valley and have been shot from the hilltop or so, that could be a situation in which you could kill a man in a fight by hitting him from the back -- in the back. Is that the kind of situation you were thinking of?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I was thinking of various situations on the basis of which one draws conclusions. But in wartime there are also kinds of situations. This is for me nothing unusual, and it doesn't lead me to doubt or suspect that this was something out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question to you is the following. The Presiding Judge read you a part of the description of body number 7. And he quoted the part of the report which makes mention of wounds on the head of that person. And you said, yes, well, if a body -- if a bullet encounters resistance and deviates from its normal trajectory, but if it encounters resistance it may cause all kinds of terrible wounds, and I understand that. But please note at the end of the description of the doctor in this case, in this case of body number 7, that he only talks about an entry at the right collar bone in this body and the exit at the back. So I don't see how this bullet could have reached the head, so to speak. He doesn't mention other bullets. Do you have an explanation? Can you help me there?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I could make a comparison as someone who deals with forensics and who is working on ballistics. When a round hits glass very often nothing is left. So one doesn't know where it entered or where it exited when the glass is on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I also have one question for the Defence because I don't remember having heard this before. But could the Defence tell us where this document comes from. Is it from the military court or is it from another archive? Maybe I have missed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this is a document that the Defence received during the investigations in the cantonal court in Zenica and the cantonal prosecutor's office in Zenica. Some of these documents and others like them were received from the prosecutor's office. And this particular one that I showed to the witness, I'm not sure from which of these three sources it came. But it is to be found in the court register and among the documents of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still talking about this document, I would like to ask the Defence, the last page of the document where we see the conclusion, just before the conclusion there's a line. Have you seen the original or is this a copy of the original?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did you say, Mr. President, that the line was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in the B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite frank, Mr. President, this is a copy of the document. As our investigators examined the documents in the courts, I personally cannot testify about the original document because we never received originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Are there any additional questions? We have a few minutes left. Does the Prosecution have any questions emanating from the Judges' questions? And then I'll give the floor to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. President, yes, I do have one question and that relates to an answer you gave in relation to the Presiding Judge's question about this -- I call it now cut or whatever, wound we saw on the videoclip.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said that, and I quote you, you "needed more precise factors on the basis of which to draw conclusions." And in an answer to Judge Swart's question you also said that the configuration of land would be important to make determinations. Can you elaborate a little bit more about this cut. What factors -- how would you have determined what the circumstances of that wound was? You as an expert in that field, how -- if you had free hands, how would you have gone about to determine the circumstances of this infliction of that wound?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: You mean this specific wound on the neck of one of the victims or generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, specifically.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: If you want my opinion, I didn't provide it previously regarding neck injuries. It is difficult on the basis of a photograph or a videotape that was shown to me on the monitor. As a specialist, when I look at this photograph it reminds me of a surface injury. Had it been deeper there would have been a very visible opening. The width of the scar would have been greater, though I'm not a forensic medical expert, but as a criminal technician that would be my opinion for that particular photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you were asked to determine what the cause of this wound was, how would you have followed up? What would you have done if you were in charge of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: This is something specific, and then I would probably know what to do. We are talking about the human body or something else, but now as we just have a photograph, or rather, a video still, we can just comment on them with a certain degree of probability. So that means --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But would you have interviewed witnesses, tried to find witnesses who were present when the infliction of the wound would have happened. Would you have tried to do that?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: A forensic medical expert or me as a ballistic expert should not engage in any kind of interviewing in order to make our decisions. Decisions are made on the basis of concrete facts and traces. Traces never lie. People may lie, but traces never lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you yourself put into the shoes of an investigative judge in order to find out what the reasons are for this wound, would you interview witnesses as an example?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: You mean as head of the investigating team, head of the entire investigations or as a technical person who did the technical part of the work? It depends on my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, the former one, the head of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Probably I would, because part of the investigations was conducted in that way, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a comment to make about this "report" you just discussed about. We received that for the first time two days ago or three days ago from the Defence. And you see as the B/C/S does not call them any, as we call them, ERN numbers. But in preparation for this witness I checked our files again and as it happens - and I just gave the originals of our files to the Defence - this expert report followed the photo identification report. And I understand we seized it somewhere some time ago. And the reason -- yes, I believe it was the result of an RFA, request for assistance. And the reason we didn't pick it up is because it's wrongly dated. It's a very shallow explanation, but if you look at the head it says "1992." And perhaps the system or whoever was dealing with it didn't pick it up as part of this investigation. It also doesn't mention Dusina, it just says in the title "Lasva, near Zenica." So we have it. It was ERN'd and I gave the original -- it's also a copy, but we have the original copy is with the Defence right now. She has the file with her. And if you want to have a look at our original, then you are very welcome to it. That's the explanation I can give you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the original there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's with Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can have a look at it straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it was a copy of what we were provided. You'll see it's not originally signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these are photocopies. These are photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Defence have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have a response to make. Clearly the source from which we obtained the document is identical with the source explained by my learned colleague from the Prosecution. And, Your Honour, you will be able to see that on page 6 of this document the same straight line appears. So certainly it exists on the original document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions from the Judges' questions. You were shown a video recording. I would like to ask you. When you took photographs of the bodies in the morgue of the Zenica hospital, in addition did you put any markings next to the bodies? And if so, are those markings visible on your photographs?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The markings we placed by the bodies, the markings 1, 2, 3, and 4. And in the document, in Exhibit Number 334, P334, the names are under those numbers, 1, 2, 3. But 3/93 has been added there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husejnagic, in response to a question you said that when you were there in the morgue you didn't have a video camera nor did anyone use a video to film the scene. And is that your response to the video shown to you by the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see anyone using a video camera to film the scene, but I think it was only in 1997 that the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, obtained a video camera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If someone had filmed the scene with a video camera while you were there and you were taking photographs of the corpses and there was a doctor who was there who described the bodies, if someone had filmed the scene would the video have picked up the numbers that you had placed by the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I think it would have been impossible to film the bodies without capturing the markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since in addition to this document which we showed to the witness, we had photocopies of photographs which weren't clear, the copies were very bad, could our colleagues from the Prosecution show us the best -- the Prosecution showed us the best version of these documents. Could we now show the witness these photographs, these copies, to determine whether these are in fact the photographs that the witness took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Usher, could you show this file to the Defence so they can take the photographs from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can show them to the witness. You could ask him to put them on the ELMO so we can all see them. Could you put the first sheet on the ELMO, please, because the witness previously said that in addition to the photographs he provided to the court there is a front page with his signature. Perhaps the witness could have a look at the front page and tell us whether the bottom of the page we can see his name and his signature, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very bottom you can't see everything but I think it's sufficient. You can see the first and last name and my colleague Hadzic Redzo is above with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us all the photographs one after another, and can you point to the markings you placed by the bodies when you photographed them. And these are the markings referred to the doctor later on.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Number 1 through 93. In the document I mentioned early on, P334.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Here we have number 2, number 3, number 4. This number is part of the equipment of the forensic -- that the forensic team has. It's used to indicate traces, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: You can -- this is number 4. Here it's not very visible, but number 5 should have been here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: I think, if you have a good look, you can see the outline of number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do continue.

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: 6, 7, 8, 9, and number 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told the Presiding Judge about the method of identification when you took the fingerprints of the right index finger and you provided certain explanations. You said you didn't see these individuals' identity cards. But could you please tell us, where are the files of all the fingerprints of the right index fingers of all those who have identity cards in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in the places where identity cards were issued, the police administrations have certain form -- certain forms for identity cards. And they have the fingerprints of the right index finger. And as a rule, if the right index finger is damaged, then you take a fingerprint from the left one. As a rule when you proceed with identifications, when you don't know who the person is, you take a fingerprint of both the right and left index finger.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when your colleague who identified the body under number 8 made such a comparison, compared the data with the data that the police administration in Zenica had?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in the files of identity cards you have the fingerprint of the -- from the right index finger. And in the course of the investigations, we took fingerprints from the right index finger of body number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Chamber also asked you a number of questions about the fact that in the case of some wounds the doctor didn't refer to the entry and exit wounds, and you said that depending on the trajectory of a bullet, a bullet can sever part of the body. And in such cases, there's no exit or entry wound. Could you please tell us, if a body has multiple wounds, is it possible that in the case of parts of the body being severed there is no entry or exit wound, whereas in the cases of other wounds inflicted on other parts of the body it's possible to detect an entry and exit wound? Did you come across any such cases?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions. I've already explained this. As I've said, the obstacles encountered by the bullet is the main factor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the photos. You said that the original photographs are in the possession of the person you forwarded them to. But does the CSB keep in its archives some of the basic material on the basis of which it might be possible to establish that these are in fact the photographs that you took?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the instructions and rules of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, the forensic department must keep negatives that were made when carrying out investigations. They must keep these negatives in their archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, although there might be an objection, but you said that you knew Mr. Turkic and he was the most professional man, most competent man in the hospital at the time. In the course of the examination -- in the course of the investigation -- in the course of the examination of the body, Dr. Turkic -- if Dr. Turkic had observed a significant kind of wound, would Dr. Turkic have referred to that wound, to such a wound, in his findings? What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ERMIN HUSEJNAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't place myself in such a situation for a number of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness can't answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You already mentioned the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not been correctly interpreted. The doctor wouldn't have placed himself in such a situation - that's what I wanted to say - in the course of such investigations. Well, I think it would have been strange if the doctor tried to misrepresent something or falsify something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the objection was obvious because it calls for speculation of what is in the mind of someone else. Also, I'm not sure whether the witness said before he was the most professional doctor. I thought he was the only doctor in the Zenica morgue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in fact the witness said that he was the only doctor in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave if the Prosecution allows us we will make better copies of these photographs, but we would wish to tender these documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has two documents they would like to have admitted into evidence: The description of the bodies under number 5, and there are the photographs as well. So we need two exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we don't have the photocopies, we'll wait until tomorrow. Does the Prosecution have any objections to having these two documents admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, not at all, Mr. President. But just if we could make the copy, because these are the originals and it's a chain of custody issue. So I'll give you the best copy I could do. Second, if we could have an official translation of this external description report because there are a couple of errors. For instance, just one example, at the end of the first page it starts in the English translation: "There is an exit wound on the right cheek." And in B/C/S it says: "There is an entry wound." So if just a good translation -- I'm sure it's a good one, but if it could be checked again. We have an official CLSS translation of this important document. Other than that, we don't have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the interpreters, the translators, in this Tribunal have a very difficult job to do and they work under pressure. Sometimes I notice errors such as the ones referred to by my colleague. This is an official Tribunal translation, but we could make a request to have this translation reviewed again in order to eliminate any errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will mark these documents for identification and then we will provide definitive numbers once we have the photocopies and the official translations. Could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH1638 is the report number. DH1638/E will be the English version. As far as the photographs are concerned, the number will be DH1639.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have marked these documents for identification. Once we have the photographs, we'll provide them with definitive numbers. And once we have the official translations, we will provide definitive numbers, too, but we will bear these documents in mind. Witness, this completes your testimony. Thank you for coming to The Hague. You have answered all the questions put to you by both parties and the Judges. We wish you a good trip home and all the best in your current career as head of the forensic department. Thank you. And if there are no other issues to be raised, I will see everyone at the hearing tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of December, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.01 p.m.,
